bigQuestion: Who decides which bodies a league counts, and what happens when a person does not fit the box?

story.title: Three Forms on One Desk
story.kicker: Every blank on an entry form was written by someone, in some year, for some reason.
paragraphs: An entry form for a high school meet sits on a coach's desk. It asks for a name, a birth date, a school and a grade. Each blank works like a gate. A student who is too old, or who attends another school, cannot pass. In Illinois, the state's high school association has kept those gates since the start of the 1900s.

A second form comes from an international wheelchair race. It asks for a sport class, written as a letter and a number. A panel of trained classifiers gave the athlete that class. The first organized wheelchair games, held at an English hospital in 1948, used no such codes at all.

A third form, from an Olympic past, once asked women for a certificate. From 1968 until the late 1990s, the International Olympic Committee checked women's chromosomes before they could compete. Men were never checked. The paper proved that a woman had passed a test the committee itself designed.

Each box on these forms was written by an organization at a particular time. People in meeting rooms voted the boxes into rule books. Later, others argued about them and rewrote them. Some rewrites came from courts, some from scandals, and some from athletes who challenged the box they were given.
story.think: Which box on a sports entry form do you think has changed the most over time, and who changed it?

lessons.title: Changing the Flag
lessons.mainIdea: Athletes compete for a country under nationality rules, and each governing body decides when an athlete may switch.
reading: An Olympic athlete does not simply sign up. The athlete must hold the *nationality*, or legal membership, of the country whose team puts them forward. The Olympic Charter, the IOC's rule book, sets the terms in its rule on nationality. An athlete who has already competed for one country usually waits three years before competing for another, unless the bodies involved agree to shorten the wait.

Zola Budd grew up in South Africa, a country then barred from Olympic sport because of apartheid. In January 1984, at seventeen, she ran 5,000 meters faster than the women's world record. The time was never ratified, because South Africa was not a member of world athletics. That April, Britain granted her *citizenship* in about two weeks, through her British grandfather, and she ran for Britain at the Los Angeles Games that summer.

The speed of Budd's passport caused a public fight in Britain. Critics said a star had jumped a line that ordinary applicants waited in for months. Supporters said her grandfather gave her a real legal claim. Soccer has its own rule book on the question. FIFA, founded in 1904, usually ties a player to one *national team* after an official senior match, though in 2020 it eased the rule for some players who had played only a few such matches when young.

words.d: legal membership in a country, which decides which national team an athlete may join
the legal status of being a member of a country, with its rights and duties
the team chosen to represent a country in international competition

look.title: Two Routes to a New Flag
look.text: Route one: an athlete moves abroad as a child, grows up there and becomes a citizen as an adult. Route two: a star athlete from a barred country gains citizenship in about two weeks through a grandparent, months before an Olympic Games. Both hold real passports. Both meet the written rule.

check.why: The Charter's nationality rule usually asks for three years since the athlete last competed for the first country.

lessons.title: Age as a Line
lessons.mainIdea: Age limits in youth, Olympic and pro sport are written rules, and breaking one can erase a result.
reading: Little League Baseball began in Williamsport, Pennsylvania, in 1939. Its founder, Carl Stotz, set an *age limit* so that children would play against others of about the same size. The Little League World Series, first held in 1947, is for players no older than twelve under its rules at the time.

In 2001 a pitcher named Danny Almonte led a team from the Bronx, New York, to the World Series. Reporters then found records in the Dominican Republic showing he was fourteen. Little League ruled him ineligible and *vacated* the team's wins from that summer. Adults, not the player, had supplied the false birth date.

Professional leagues also draw age lines. After Red Grange signed with the Chicago Bears in 1925, days after his last game for the University of Illinois, the NFL adopted a rule against signing players before their college class graduated. In 2004 running back Maurice Clarett sued over the NFL's version of that rule. A federal appeals court upheld it because it was part of *collective bargaining* between the league and its players' union.

Gymnastics drew its own line. In 1997 the International Gymnastics Federation raised the minimum age for senior events, including the Olympics, to sixteen in the year of competition. One member of China's bronze-medal women's team at the 2000 Sydney Games was later found to have been fourteen. In 2010 the IOC took the team's bronze medal away and awarded it to the United States.

words.d: a rule setting the youngest or oldest age allowed to compete
officially erased, as when wins or titles are removed from the record
talks in which a union and employers agree on rules for pay and work

Both lines were broken by false birth records, and both times a result was taken away years or weeks later.

lessons.title: Weight Classes and a Hard Winter
lessons.mainIdea: Wrestling sorts bodies by weight, and three college deaths in 1997 forced new rules on how athletes make weight.
reading: In wrestling, a *weight class* groups athletes within a set range of body weight, so that people of similar size meet. Each athlete must pass a *weigh-in*, an official check on a scale, before competing. Modern Olympic wrestling has used weight classes since the early 1900s, and school and college wrestling in the United States adopted the same system.

Weight classes also create pressure to lose weight quickly before a weigh-in. In late 1997, three college wrestlers died within about six weeks while trying to drop weight fast. They wrestled for schools in North Carolina, Wisconsin and Michigan. Their deaths drew national attention and led to federal and medical studies of rapid weight loss in the sport.

The NCAA rewrote its rules for the 1998–99 season. It banned rubber suits, saunas and other ways of sweating off weight, and it moved weigh-ins closer to the start of competition. It also raised the limits of its weight classes. In the 2000s the national high school federation added a program that sets each wrestler's *minimum weight* for the season, based on a body-fat and hydration test.

words.d: a group of athletes within a set range of body weight who compete against each other
an official check of an athlete's weight on a scale before competing
the lowest weight a wrestler may compete at in a season, set by a health test

look.title: A Scale Before the Match
look.text: A weight class promises a fair match between people of similar size. But the scale reads only once, at the weigh-in. Before 1998, a college wrestler could lose several pounds in the hours before stepping on it, then regain them before competing. The new rules of 1998 moved the scale closer to the match and banned the fastest ways of shedding weight.

check.why: The program uses a body-fat and hydration test to set a lowest allowed weight for the season.

lessons.title: A Racer Sues Her School
lessons.mainIdea: In 2006 wheelchair racer Tatyana McFadden sued to race alongside her high school teammates, and Maryland then wrote a new law.
reading: Tatyana McFadden was born in Russia in 1989 with spina bifida, a condition of the spine that affects the legs. She spent her early years in an orphanage and was adopted by an American family, who brought her to Maryland. At fifteen she won a silver and a bronze medal in wheelchair racing at the 2004 Paralympic Games in Athens.

At Atholton High School in Howard County, Maryland, she joined the track team. School officials had her race in separate *heats*, alone on the track, and her results did not count toward team scores. In 2006 she and her mother sued the school system under federal disability law. A federal judge granted an *injunction*, an order that she be allowed to race on the track at the same time as the other runners.

The case did not end with one athlete. In 2008 Maryland passed the Fitness and Athletics Equity for Students with Disabilities Act. In its title, *equity* means fairness in giving each student a real chance. It required school systems to give students with disabilities fair chances to take part in physical education and school sports, including adapted and combined teams. McFadden went on to win many Paralympic gold medals and major marathon titles.

words.d: separate rounds of a race, each run by a smaller group of athletes
a court order that tells someone to do, or stop doing, a certain thing
fairness in giving people what they need to have an equal chance

check.why: The Fitness and Athletics Equity for Students with Disabilities Act required fair chances in PE and sports.

lessons.title: Arguing Over a Class
lessons.mainIdea: Paralympic sport draws lines for who is eligible and who shares a class, and athletes can challenge where those lines fall.
reading: Early disability sport grouped athletes by medical diagnosis, with separate classes for each group. That produced many events with only a few entrants each. From the late 1980s, many sports moved to *functional classification*. It asks how much an impairment limits the actions a sport needs, so athletes with different conditions can share one class.

Every sport also sets *minimum impairment criteria*, the least impairment an athlete must have to be eligible at all. The IPC recognizes ten eligible impairment types, including impaired muscle power, limb deficiency, vision impairment and intellectual impairment. Each sport draws its own line, so an athlete who is not eligible in one sport may still be eligible in another.

A class is not always final. Some athletes hold a class marked for review, often because they are young or their condition can change. Athletes and coaches may file protests. The IPC's rules also punish *intentional misrepresentation*, meaning an athlete pretending during testing to have more impairment than they really have.

Disputes are common. Athletes in several sports have said publicly that rivals were placed in classes where they faced people with more impairment. The IPC has answered by calling for evidence-based classification. That means funding research that measures, sport by sport, how each impairment affects performance.

words.d: grouping athletes by how an impairment affects the actions of a sport
the least impairment an athlete must have to be eligible in a sport
pretending during classification to have more impairment than one has

look.prompt: What evidence should a classification panel look at before deciding the protest?

check.why: Grouping by effect on the sport let athletes with different conditions share classes.

lessons.title: Sydney 2000 and a Broken Class
lessons.mainIdea: A cheating scandal at the 2000 Paralympics led to intellectual impairment events being suspended for twelve years.
reading: Spain's basketball team won gold in the *intellectual impairment* event at the 2000 Paralympic Games in Sydney, Australia. A few weeks later, a Spanish journalist who had played on the team revealed the truth. Most of the players had no intellectual impairment at all. No one had checked their papers with care.

Spain's Paralympic committee returned the medals. The International Paralympic Committee then suspended every event for athletes with intellectual impairment. The suspension hurt thousands of honest athletes around the world who had done nothing wrong. It showed that a class is only as fair as the *verification* behind it.

Rebuilding took more than a decade. Sports bodies worked with researchers to design tests that measured how intellectual impairment affects a specific sport. Athletes now needed records showing that the impairment began before age eighteen. At the London 2012 Paralympics, athletes with intellectual impairment returned in three sports: athletics, swimming and table tennis.

words.d: a lasting difference in learning and reasoning that begins in childhood, one of the Paralympic impairment types
checking that the facts on a form or record are true
stopped for a time, with the chance of starting again later

lessons.title: A Golf Cart at the Supreme Court
lessons.mainIdea: In 2001 the Supreme Court ruled that disability law required the PGA Tour to let Casey Martin ride a cart.
reading: Casey Martin grew up in Oregon and played golf at Stanford University. He was born with Klippel-Trenaunay-Weber syndrome, a circulation disorder in his right leg. Walking a full course caused him pain and put his leg at serious risk. In 1997 he asked the PGA Tour to let him ride a cart in its events.

The Tour said walking was part of the test of skill at the top level and refused. Martin sued under the *Americans with Disabilities Act* of 1990. A federal court in Oregon ruled for him in 1998, and a federal appeals court agreed in 2000. The Tour then took the case to the U.S. Supreme Court.

In PGA Tour, Inc. v. Martin (2001), the Court ruled 7–2 that a cart was a *reasonable modification* the law required. Justice John Paul Stevens wrote that walking was not essential to golf itself. In a *dissent*, Justice Antonin Scalia argued that a sports body should make its own rules and that judges should not decide what is essential to a game.

The ruling also settled a split between courts. In 2000 a federal appeals court in Chicago had ruled for the U.S. Golf Association in a similar case brought by another golfer, Ford Olinger. After the Martin decision, the Supreme Court sent that case back to be looked at again.

words.d: a 1990 federal law that bars discrimination against people with disabilities in many public places and services
an adjustment the law requires so an athlete with a disability can play, unless it would alter the core of the game
a written opinion by a judge who disagrees with the court's decision

check.why: The Court ruled 7–2 that a cart was a reasonable modification the ADA required.

check.why: Scalia argued that judges should not decide what is essential to a game.

check.why: A dissent is written by a judge who disagrees with the majority.

lessons.title: Blades Before the Court
lessons.mainIdea: Runners on prostheses have challenged track's governing body in a sports court, with different results in 2008 and 2020.
reading: Oscar Pistorius of South Africa had both legs amputated below the knee as a baby. He raced on carbon-fiber *prostheses*, often called blades. In January 2008 the International Association of Athletics Federations, now World Athletics, ruled that the blades gave him an advantage and barred him from able-bodied events. Its ruling relied on a study it had ordered from a German university.

Pistorius appealed to the *Court of Arbitration for Sport*, an international sports court the IOC set up in 1984. In May 2008 the court overturned the ban. It found that the evidence did not prove his blades gave him an overall advantage. At the 2012 London Olympics he ran the 400 meters and the 4 × 400 meter relay, the first double-leg amputee to run in Olympic track.

Later cases went differently. German long jumper Markus Rehm, who jumps on a prosthesis, won a German national title against non-disabled jumpers in 2014, but he was left off Germany's team for that summer's European Championships. American sprinter Blake Leeper challenged a World Athletics rule limiting the height of running blades. In 2020 the sports court upheld the height rule for Leeper, but it struck down the part that put the *burden of proof* on athletes to show they had no advantage.

words.d: artificial body parts, such as legs, that replace missing limbs
an international sports court, created by the IOC in 1984, that hears appeals from athletes and federations
the duty to prove a claim; whoever carries it loses if the evidence is unclear

lessons.title: Certificates and Chromosomes
lessons.mainIdea: From 1968 to the late 1990s the IOC screened every female Olympian's chromosomes, a practice many scientists criticized.
reading: Women first competed at the Olympic Games in Paris in 1900, in tennis and golf. Women's track and field events were added in Amsterdam in 1928. From the start, sports bodies kept women's events separate. By the 1960s, officials began asking how to decide who could enter the women's category.

At the 1966 European Championships in Budapest, officials required female athletes to undergo a physical inspection. In 1967 Polish sprinter Ewa Kłobukowska, an Olympic relay champion, was barred after a *chromosome* test. At the 1968 Winter Games in Grenoble and Summer Games in Mexico City, the IOC began screening women with a cheek-cell test. Those who passed received a certificate.

Geneticists warned that the test was flawed. Some women had chromosome patterns that differ from the typical pattern yet had no athletic advantage from them. Spanish hurdler María José Martínez-Patiño was ruled out after a test in 1985. She fought the ruling and was allowed to compete again in 1988.

The track federation ended *screening* of all women in the early 1990s. The IOC stopped universal *sex verification* before the Sydney Games of 2000. It kept the power to look at individual cases. That choice moved the debate from a single lab test to rules written case by case.

words.d: a thread-like structure in cells that carries genes
testing everyone in a group, not only people who raise a question
testing used by sports bodies to decide who may enter the women's category

check.why: Geneticists warned the test flagged women whose chromosome patterns gave no athletic advantage.

lessons.title: Testosterone Before the Courts
lessons.mainIdea: Rules limiting testosterone in the women's category have been fought over by athletes, federations and courts since 2009.
reading: In 2009, eighteen-year-old Caster Semenya of South Africa won the 800 meters at the world championships in Berlin. The track federation, then called the IAAF, ordered her to undergo sex testing. Her private results were leaked to the press. She was kept out of races for about eleven months before being cleared in 2010.

In 2011 the IAAF adopted rules on *hyperandrogenism*, meaning naturally high levels of *testosterone*. Women above a set level had to lower it to compete. Indian sprinter Dutee Chand challenged the rules at the Court of Arbitration for Sport. In 2015 the court suspended them for two years and asked the federation to prove the advantage with evidence.

In 2018 the IAAF issued new rules for athletes with *differences of sex development*, or DSD. They covered races from 400 meters to the mile. In 2019 the sports court upheld them. It called them discriminatory but said they were necessary to protect fair competition. Swiss courts refused to overturn that ruling in 2020. In 2023 World Athletics widened the rules to every event.

Semenya took her case to the European Court of Human Rights, which ruled in her favor in 2023 and again, on narrower grounds, in 2025. The federation says the rules protect a fair female category. Critics include many doctors and human rights groups. They say the rules single out a small number of women, many from Africa and Asia. They also say the rules push these women toward medical treatment they did not ask for.

words.d: a hormone that affects muscle, bone and other body traits
naturally high levels of hormones such as testosterone
conditions in which a person's chromosomes, hormones or body develop in less typical ways; shortened to DSD

look.title: Two Arguments, One Rule
look.text: A federation argues: the women's category exists so that women can win, and high testosterone gives an edge in some events. An athlete argues: I was born this way, I have always lived as a woman, and the rule asks me to change my body to keep my job. The sports court in 2019 agreed the rule was discriminatory but still upheld it.
look.prompt: What evidence would each side need to show to win the argument? How did the 2019 court weigh the two?

check.why: In 2015 the court suspended the hyperandrogenism rules for two years and asked the IAAF for evidence.

choices: They were discriminatory but necessary for fair competition.

check.why: The 2019 ruling called the rules discriminatory but upheld them as necessary.

check.why: Hyperandrogenism means naturally high levels of androgen hormones such as testosterone.

lessons.title: Policies for the Female Category
lessons.mainIdea: Rules on transgender athletes in the female category have changed many times since 2004, and many bodies now write their own.
reading: Since 1975, federal Title IX rules have let U.S. schools keep separate boys' and girls' teams in many sports. That long-standing split is why the question of who may join the girls' or women's team carries so much weight. For decades the question drew little public debate. From the 2000s onward it reached sports federations, state lawmakers and courts.

The IOC first wrote rules for *transgender* athletes in 2004. That policy required surgery, legal recognition and two years of hormone therapy. In 2015 the IOC dropped the surgery rule and set a testosterone limit instead. At the 2021 Tokyo Games, New Zealand weightlifter Laurel Hubbard became the first openly transgender woman to compete in an individual Olympic event.

Late in 2021, the IOC issued a *framework* that stopped setting one rule for all sports and left eligibility to each international federation. In 2022 the swimming federation, now World Aquatics, barred transgender women who had gone through male puberty from its women's events. World Athletics adopted a similar rule in 2023. In 2025 World Athletics began requiring a one-time gene test for athletes entering women's events.

U.S. states have also written laws. Idaho passed the first state law limiting girls' and women's school teams by sex at birth in 2020, and many other states followed. In February 2025 a presidential executive order took the same position, and the NCAA changed its policy. Supporters of such rules speak of fairness and safety in the *female category*. Opponents speak of inclusion and the harm of shutting students out of school life.

words.d: the division of a sport set aside for women and girls
a set of guiding principles that bodies use when writing their own rules
describing a person whose gender identity differs from the sex recorded at birth

look.title: Who Writes the Line
look.text: In 2015 one body, the IOC, set a single testosterone limit for every Olympic sport. In 2021 the IOC handed that choice to each sport's international federation. Swimming wrote its rule in 2022 and track and field in 2023. Meanwhile, U.S. states and the federal government wrote their own rules for school teams.
